title: Life cycles
exam_coverage_note: Area A (LOs 1-4) accounts for 15-20% of exam marks.
apm_learning_objective: Understand the distinct life cycle stages used to structure and organise a project.
learning_outcomes: 1a) Understand the distinctive features of linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles (including why projects are structured as phases in linear life cycles) and know when each is applicable.
1b) Knowledge of the differences between a project life cycle and an extended life cycle.
1c) Understand how the context and culture of an organisation, and the needs of a specific project, influence the choice of life cycle and any adaptations that may be needed to the life cycle.
1d) Knowledge of the strengths and limitations of different life cycles.
where_this_fits: The life cycle is the first structural decision on a project, and nearly everything else inherits from it. Choose linear and you get gated phases, fixed scope and formal change control. Choose iterative and you get evolving scope, rapid feedback and a different risk process entirely. That single choice reaches into governance, reviews, benefits, resourcing, risk and change control. Several of which ask you directly how a process differs between linear and iterative. Get life cycles solid here and you are part-way through four other learning objectives.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A framework comprising a series of distinct phases required to transform an idea into reality in an orderly and efficient manner.
key_definitions.plain_english: The set of stages a project moves through from first idea to finished output. It is the skeleton everything else hangs on.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that takes the project through a set of distinct, sequential phases in a single pass, only progressing from phase to phase once all the work on the current phase is completed.
key_definitions.plain_english: One pass, in order, finish each phase before starting the next. Sometimes called 'waterfall'.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that takes the project through a set of repeatable phases to create an initial output, which is then built upon with further deliveries of incremental value.
key_definitions.plain_english: Build a first working version, then keep improving it in repeated cycles as you learn more.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that blends the philosophies, principles, tools and techniques of both linear and iterative life cycles to suit a particular project.
key_definitions.plain_english: Mix and match. Commonly iterative early where uncertainty is high, linear later once scope is settled.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A life cycle that adds adoption and benefits realisation phases to the end of a standard project life cycle.
key_definitions.plain_english: The project does not stop at handover. The team stays accountable until the change is embedded and the benefits show up.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The process of ensuring that benefits are derived from delivered outputs and outcomes.
key_definitions.plain_english: Checking the value actually arrived, rather than assuming it did because the thing got built.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The overarching values, principles and behaviours the project works to throughout its delivery.
key_definitions.plain_english: How the team agrees to operate: agreed before picking frameworks or tools, not after.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A timeboxed iteration with a fixed end date.
key_definitions.plain_english: A short, fixed-length work cycle. The end date does not move; the scope inside it does.

key_definitions.apm_definition: An initial output delivered rapidly, with additional scope items assessed, prioritised and planned for in future iterations.
key_definitions.plain_english: The smallest useful thing you can put in front of users to start learning from them.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Adoption and use of outputs creates improved business outcomes, with those outcomes going on to generate the anticipated business benefit.
key_definitions.plain_english: Output = the thing you built. Outcome = what changes because people use it. Benefit = the measurable value that change creates.

core_content.outcome_title: Linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles
core_content.body_markdown:
## Phases: why projects are structured this way
Phases exist for three reasons, and it pays to learn them as three named reasons rather than a vague sense that phases are tidy.

| Reason | What it buys you |
|---|---|
| Better grouping of activities | Phases group work by type (analysis, planning, building) so the right people are on the right kind of work at the right time. |
| More accurate plans and estimates | Smaller chunks are easier to plan and estimate, which raises both accuracy and confidence. |
| Tracking and monitoring progress | Phases create clear break points to measure against checkpoints and milestones, so you can see early whether things are on track. |

Every project passes through the same high-level phases whichever life cycle is used. The life cycle decides *how* you move through them, not whether they exist.

## Life cycle approaches: only two at the top level
There are only two at the top level. Everything else blends them.

Linear runs distinct, sequential phases in a single pass. You move on only once the current phase is complete.

Iterative runs repeatable phases. You create an initial output, then build on it with further deliveries of incremental value as the solution evolves.

Hybrid is a deliberate blend, because most real environments are messy enough that neither pure approach fits end to end.

## Linear: the phases, and the control they buy

Because each phase finishes before the next begins, linear gives tight control over progression and a clear framework for scheduling, budgeting, resourcing and risk.

The boundaries matter as much as the phases. Gateways are what they create, and a gateway is where milestones, governance and reviews live. No gateway, nowhere to put the decision.

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Concept | An idea (exploiting an opportunity or solving a problem) is analysed for viability and fit with organisational objectives. Research, high-level requirements, often an outline business case. |
| Definition | How to make it real is planned: detailed analysis, estimation, planning and a fuller statement of requirements, ending in the sponsor's approval to proceed. |
| Deployment | Plans are implemented. Testing and assurance monitor performance to keep intended outcomes and benefits on track. |
| Transition | Outputs are accepted and transitioned into use, handover, then formal closure. |

Naming and phasing vary by organisation, shaped by its nature, purpose, environment and governance culture. Smaller projects often use a shorter cycle.

Fits best: clearly defined or high-risk projects, where time, cost and risk can flex to protect agreed scope and quality, and projects with a high cost of change, where extra rigour up front pays for itself.

## Iterative: how it actually works

Iterative rests on continuous improvement and evolutionary development: the solution evolves as learning takes place and new information emerges.

You start with a high-level vision. Detail is defined and built inside each cycle. Because specification and design run in parallel, deployment is fast-tracked and users get value earlier, which produces rapid feedback you can act on.

A common structure comes from the dynamic systems development method (DSDM):

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Pre-project and feasibility | The idea is established, aligned to objectives, cost effective, technically possible, with a clear measurable goal. |
| Foundations | Planning and design: a high-level delivery plan and a technical design. |
| Evolutionary development and deployment | Repeatable cycles of detailed design, development, testing and deployment. Early cycles produce an initial output; later ones add value as learning emerges. |
| Realisation | Embed the outputs and evolve the next iteration. |

Many iterative life cycles use sprints: timeboxed iterations with a fixed end date, typically producing a minimum viable product first, with further scope assessed, prioritised and planned into later iterations. A daily scrum keeps the team synchronised.

Fits best: new or innovative work without detailed up-front knowledge, prototypes and pioneering technology, and situations with a low cost of change so the project can pivot quickly.

What it demands: collaboration and co-creation. It runs on engagement and regular feedback from end users, and works best with co-located teams, which keeps communication barriers down.

## Hybrid: blending the two

There is no one-size-fits-all life cycle. A hybrid takes the useful parts of each for a specific project.

The common pattern: iterative through concept and definition to work through early uncertainty, then linear for deployment and transition once there is clarity. Stakeholders get certainty on scope; the project gets structure for controlling schedule, budget, quality and risk.

You are not locked in. Many successful projects adapt as they go.

What makes hybrid work or fail is alignment with the organisation's wider governance, reporting, change control, roles and responsibilities, and dependencies on other initiatives. Blend the life cycles without aligning governance and you get two systems of working arguing with each other.

exam_tips.heading: Phases: why projects are structured this way
exam_tips.tip: The syllabus asks for this in so many words, so have all three ready: grouping of activities, accuracy of plans and estimates, and tracking of progress. An answer that says phases keep the work tidy scores nothing.

exam_tips.heading: Linear: the phases, and the control they buy
exam_tips.tip: Cost of change is the quickest route into a linear answer. You cannot un-build a stadium, so the rigour goes in before anyone digs. Name the phase boundary the decision sits at and you have turned a definition into an application mark.

exam_tips.heading: Iterative: how it actually works
exam_tips.tip: Sprint, MVP, scrum and DSDM are the four names to have ready, and a scenario that mentions evolving scope with fast feedback is asking for them. What iterative demands is the half people leave out: no sustained user engagement, no iterative delivery.

exam_tips.heading: Hybrid: blending the two
exam_tips.tip: Hybrid questions are rarely about the blend itself. They are about governance, because one set of reporting, change control and roles has to cover both halves. Write that sentence and you have the mark most answers miss.

worked_examples.heading: Linear: the phases, and the control they buy
worked_examples.situation: You are 14 weeks into a 30-week office refit, in deployment. The client wants the reception layout redesigned.
worked_examples.ask: Do you refuse because linear is fixed?
worked_examples.answer: No, you run it through formal change control and price the rework. Linear does not block change, it makes the cost visible before anyone commits. The walls are already up, so the cost of change is high.

core_content.outcome_title: Project life cycle vs extended life cycle
core_content.body_markdown:
## Project vs extended life cycle: where each one stops
A standard project life cycle ends once the agreed outputs are deployed and handed over. An extended life cycle adds two phases on the end.

| Added phase | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Adoption | Communications, training, knowledge sharing and change management, so operational teams actually use the outputs correctly. |
| Benefits realisation | Measuring business performance to confirm adoption is producing the intended outcomes and the anticipated benefits. |

They typically run in parallel, not one after the other. As adoption rises, outcomes improve, and benefits follow.

## Outputs, outcomes and benefits: the chain that connects them
> A new software tool is delivered (output), customer usage increases (outcome), service delivery costs fall (benefit).

Delivering the output guarantees none of the rest. That is the entire argument for extending.

## Benefits measurement: how it actually happens
This is what the extra phases actually do:

- Benefits planning is where the groundwork is laid, early rather than at the end: activities and resources for transition into use, testing schedules, acceptance criteria, quality assurance thresholds.
- Benefit owners and change managers stay active for the project's whole duration, readying the business to take the outputs.
- Measurement varies by benefit type: quantitative for operational and financial benefits, qualitative (such as user feedback) for non-financial ones.
- The project sponsor is ultimately accountable for the measurement process being robust, usually through formal benefits realisation reviews.
- If benefits are not landing, there are two honest moves: drive adoption harder, or reset the target.

## Benefits timing: how it differs by life cycle
Benefits do not arrive at the same point in every life cycle:

- Linear: benefits are usually realised at the end, once all outputs are delivered.
- Iterative: benefits are realised incrementally, as the project progresses.

## Extending the life cycle: when it makes sense
Programmes normally include adoption and benefits realisation as standard. For a standalone project it is a real trade-off:

| For extending | Against extending |
|---|---|
| Higher adoption rates | The organisation pays for project professionals' time on those activities |
| Better chance the benefits are realised, often what stakeholders judge success on | Operational teams could manage it instead |
| The project team learns how their work actually lands in the business | |

A project inside a larger programme may only need to deliver outputs, because the programme handles adoption and benefits.

Timing matters. If you are going to extend, plan for it in the early phases: the requirements, work, resources and risks of the extra phases all belong in the project management plan from the start.

exam_tips.tip: This one is directly examinable and easy to miss. If the scenario has value reaching users part way through, the life cycle is iterative and the benefits land incrementally, not at handover.

exam_tips.tip: Two words settle most of these. Programme, and adoption and benefits are already covered, so the project delivers outputs and stops. Standalone, and you are expected to weigh both columns before you land on one.

worked_examples.heading: Extending the life cycle: when it makes sense
worked_examples.situation: A CRM rollout worth 600,000 pounds hands over in March. The sponsor wants the project team released the same week, leaving training to the service desk.
worked_examples.answer: Extend. Outputs sitting unused produce no benefit, and adoption is what turns the tool into lower service costs. Essentially, eight weeks of project time is cheaper than a system nobody logs into.

core_content.outcome_title: How context and culture drive the choice
core_content.body_markdown:
## Project approach: the four factors that set it
Before choosing a life cycle, teams agree a project approach: the values, principles and behaviours the project works to. Four factors shape it.

| Factor | The question it asks |
|---|---|
| Risk appetite | How much risk is the project willing to take? Usually inherited from the organisation and its industry. |
| Cost of change | How easy is it to pivot mid-deployment? Rewriting software code is cheap. Demolishing and rebuilding a football stadium is not. |
| Business agility | Is the organisation flexible, resilient and adaptable, or rigid and bureaucratic? |
| Decision-making autonomy | Is the team empowered to decide, or does everything need layers of approval? |

The pattern worth memorising:

- High risk appetite, low cost of change, team autonomy and strong business agility give you fast progress and learning by trial and error, which points to iterative.
- Low risk appetite, high cost of change, low autonomy and low agility mean the team cannot afford mistakes, so the work turns controlled, cautious and methodical, which points to linear.

A project's approach is not black and white. It moves along a spectrum of agility, risk taking and autonomy as the project progresses.

## Project type: how well do you know the what and the how?

Turner and Cochrane's goals-and-methods matrix asks two questions, how well do we know *what* we are doing, and how well do we know *how* we will do it?

| Type | Goals | Methods | Example | What to do about it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (earth) | Clear | Clear | Large engineering | Keep concept and planning brief; deliver quickly |
| 2 (water) | Clear | Unclear | Product development | Focus early effort on the 'what' via a clear business case |
| 3 (fire) | Unclear | Clear | Software development | Move fast through concept; experiment between definition and deployment |
| 4 (air) | Unclear | Unclear | Organisational development | Spend longer in concept and definition to gain information and confidence |

High uncertainty justifies more time in concept and definition, which is what the type 4 row sets out.

## Organisational culture: the unwritten rules
Culture is the unwritten set of rules shaping behaviour and attitudes. Cameron and Quinn's model splits it on two competing pairs, stability vs flexibility, and inward vs outward looking.

| Culture | Character | Life cycle implication |
|---|---|---|
| Clan (inward/flexible) | Collaborative, nurturing, family feel, coaching leadership | Supports collaboration and co-creation |
| Adhocracy (outward/flexible) | Energetic, entrepreneurial, innovation and risk taking welcome | Iterative projects often have a strong element of adhocracy culture |
| Hierarchy (inward/stable) | Rigid, strong order and control, consistency over creativity | Suits projects under strict governance, points to linear |
| Market (outward/stable) | Results-orientated, competitive, focused on profit and market share | Creates rivalry between project teams |

Culture also varies *within* an organisation, regional offices, functions, departments and project teams develop their own subcultures.

## Adapting the life cycle: normal, not a planning failure
Adaptation is normal, not a planning failure.

- Phasing and naming change by organisation, shaped by its nature, purpose, environment and governance culture. Smaller projects often use a shorter cycle.
- The approach can change mid-project. Projects move in and out of stability, uncertainty and risk, and the approach should adapt with the environment and stakeholders' needs.
- Blending scales upwards to programmes and portfolios, iterative deployment lets a programme realise benefits earlier through rapid user feedback.

The constraint on all of it: whatever you adapt must stay aligned with organisational governance, reporting, change control, clear roles, and visible dependencies on other initiatives.

exam_tips.heading: Project approach: the four factors that set it
exam_tips.tip: Those four factors are the most reliable thing to reason from in a scenario question. Quote the two or three the scenario actually hands you, then name the life cycle they point at. Naming the factor earns more than naming the life cycle.

exam_tips.heading: Project type: how well do you know the what and the how?
exam_tips.tip: Type 4 is the exam-useful row, because it hands you a concrete reason you can point at in a scenario answer. Spending longer in concept reads as delay until you name the uncertainty it buys down.

worked_examples.heading: Project approach: the four factors that set it
worked_examples.situation: Two projects start on Monday: a 40,000-seat stadium roof, and a mobile app for the same club.
worked_examples.ask: Same organisation, same risk appetite, so why do they get different life cycles?
worked_examples.answer: Cost of change splits them. Concrete poured wrong costs millions and months, so the stadium goes linear with the rigour up front. App code is cheap to rewrite, so the app goes iterative and learns from real users.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Life cycle comparison: strengths and limitations
| Life cycle | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | Tight control of progression; clear framework for scheduling, budgeting, resourcing and risk; clear gateways for milestones, governance and reviews; suits a high cost of change | Assumes a lot of knowledge up front; poor fit for developing or changeable environments; users wait longer for value; limited scope for major change once delivery is complete |
| Iterative | Value delivered earlier; rapid user feedback; adapts as learning emerges; suits innovation, prototypes and pioneering technology; suits a low cost of change | Depends on sustained user engagement and regular feedback; works best with co-located teams; less up-front certainty on total scope, time and cost |
| Hybrid | Pragmatic mix tailored to the project; resolves early uncertainty while keeping later control; can adapt as the project progresses | Needs greater skill and clarity to run two ways of working; must be aligned to organisational governance or reporting and change control break down |
| Extended | Higher adoption rates; better chance benefits are realised, often what stakeholders judge success on; the team learns how its work lands | Additional cost for project professionals' time; must be planned from the early phases, not bolted on |

## The trade-off: one line for each life cycle
- Linear buys control and pays for it in flexibility.
- Iterative buys adaptability and pays for it in certainty.
- Hybrid buys fit and pays for it in complexity.
- Extended buys benefits and pays for it in cost.

exam_tips.heading: The trade-off: one line for each life cycle
exam_tips.tip: If you can state the cost as fluently as the strength, you understand the life cycle. However, most answers give three strengths and no limitation, which leaves half the question unanswered.

worked_examples.heading: Life cycle comparison: strengths and limitations
worked_examples.situation: Your board signs off a hybrid: iterative discovery, linear build. Six weeks in, discovery reports in two-week increments and build reports monthly against a stage gate.
worked_examples.answer: Not the blend, the governance. Hybrid needs one reporting and change control system covering both halves, or the board is reading two different pictures. That is the skill cost hybrid charges.

misconceptions.wrong: Iterative is the modern approach and is therefore better.
misconceptions.right: Neither is better. Each suits different conditions, cost of change, information available up front, risk appetite, and how much the project depends on user feedback.
They handle change through formal change control. What they handle badly is continuously evolving scope, especially once delivery is well advanced.

misconceptions.wrong: An extended life cycle just means a longer project.
misconceptions.right: It means two specific phases were added (adoption and benefits realisation) and the project team stayed accountable through them.

misconceptions.wrong: Once you have chosen a life cycle you are committed to it.
misconceptions.right: The approach can change as the project progresses, and often should. Projects move in and out of stability, uncertainty and risk.

misconceptions.wrong: Hybrid is the easy option because you can do whatever you like.
misconceptions.right: Hybrid demands more skill, because two ways of working must be reconciled with one set of governance, reporting and change control.

misconceptions.wrong: Delivering the output means the project delivered its benefits.
misconceptions.right: Outputs do not automatically generate benefit. Adoption creates outcomes, and outcomes generate benefits. Each step has to actually happen.

misconceptions.wrong: You must never use the word 'waterfall'.
misconceptions.right: The Body of Knowledge itself notes that linear life cycles are often referred to as waterfall. 'Linear' is the primary term and the safer one to lead with, but the word is not forbidden.

memory_aids.expansion: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. In that order.
Plus Adoption and Benefits realisation: the extended life cycle.

memory_aids.acronym: Built it, used it, worth it
memory_aids.expansion: Output, outcome, benefit. Always that order.
High cost of change points to linear. Low points to iterative.

progress_checkpoint: I can give the three reasons projects are structured as phases, grouping activities, more accurate estimates, tracking progress.
I can name the two fundamental approaches, linear and iterative, explain how hybrid relates to them, and list the four linear phases in order.
I can explain what phase boundaries are for: they create the gateways where milestones, governance and reviews sit.
I can describe the iterative cycle and explain what sprints and an MVP are for.
I can state the two phases an extended life cycle adds, and explain why adoption and benefits realisation run in parallel.
I can distinguish output, outcome and benefit with an example, and explain how benefits timing differs between linear and iterative.

I can name the four factors that set a project's approach (risk appetite, cost of change, business agility, decision-making autonomy) and explain how organisational culture pushes the choice either way.
I can state one strength and one limitation for each of linear, iterative and hybrid, and justify a life cycle choice using specific details from a scenario.

source_confidence.claim: Turner and Cochrane goals-and-methods matrix, including the earth / water / fire / air type labels and the worked examples for each.
source_confidence.risk: None on the facts. Noted because the memory aid built on it was removed on 2026-08-02 for being confusing: it named the four elements without encoding which dimension was unclear in each. The matrix itself stays in the body content.
